extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the USPTO eligibility analysis under 35 U.S.C. §101 (MPEP §2106), including Step 1 (statutory category) and Step 2A (Alice/Mayo two-prong inquiry) determinations. Focused on how to identify statutory categories, judicial exceptions, and when claims are directed to those exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1 – Statutory Category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim as a whole falls within one of the four statutory categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. Evaluation should be made after determining what the inventor has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO), the claim is non-statutory and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If the claim's BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-statutory subject matter and fails Step 1. Best practice: point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments. See MPEP §2106 subsection II and §2111 for BRI guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Form Paragraphs and Examiner Practice on Step 1 Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is clearly not within a statutory category and must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101, examination procedure requires use of specified form paragraphs and recommending amendments when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Step 1: NO, use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 (see MPEP §2106.07(a)(1)). If the claim fails Step 1 but applicant's disclosure suggests the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, continue analysis to determine if an amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C and recommend amendment where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2A – Directed to a Judicial Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: After establishing the claim is to a statutory category, determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon). Step 2A is the first part of the Alice/Mayo framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should be made after reviewing the entire disclosure and construing the claims under BRI. Step 2A determines whether the claim as a whole is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) requiring further Step 2B analysis, or is not directed to an exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Two-Prong Inquiry – Prong One: Recitation of a Judicial Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One asks whether the claim recites (sets forth or describes) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon. 'Recite' includes both setting forth and describing; distinct from merely 'involving' an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the specific claim limitation(s) that the examiner believes recites an exception and determine whether those limitations fall within an exception. Examples: a claim explicitly stating F=ma 'sets forth' a law of nature (recites an exception); a teeter-totter claim that merely involves mechanical principles does not 'recite' the law. If Prong One is answered NO (claim does not recite an exception), claim is eligible at Pathway B without further eligibility analysis. See MPEP §2106.04(a)-(c) for details on identifying each type of exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Two-Prong Inquiry – Prong Two: Integration into a Practical Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two asks whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application of that exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If not, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires Step 2B analysis. Mere recitation of an exception (e.g., a mathematical formula) triggers Prong One, but does not by itself mean the claim is 'directed to' the exception. Additional elements that are merely another judicial exception or merely conventional do not integrate the exception. The additional elements must 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application (Alice Corp.). See MPEP §2106.04(d)(2) for evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that Additional Elements Provide More than Another Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional claim elements that are solely other judicial exceptions do not integrate the exception into a practical application and are insufficient for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding one abstract idea to another, or relying on the unpatentable law of nature itself, cannot render the claim non-abstract. If no additional elements exist, the claim cannot be eligible. Examiners should recommend amendments where possible to resolve eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Multiple Judicial Exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may recite multiple judicial exceptions; the same eligibility analysis applies regardless of the number of exceptions recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless clearly distinct exceptions exist, avoid parsing the claim into multiple exceptions; where possible, treat the claim as containing a single judicial exception for Prong Two and Step 2B analysis. If distinct exceptions are present, examiners may select one for efficiency and analyze based on that selected exception. If the analysis shows integration into a practical application or that additional elements amount to significantly more than the selected exception, the claim is eligible; otherwise it is ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption Concern and Use of Alice/Mayo Framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Preemption is the underlying concern motivating judicial exceptions, but preemption is not a standalone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of preemption are inherent in and resolved by the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B). The absence of complete preemption does not prove eligibility; conversely, a claim that preempts an exception may be ineligible. Use the Alice/Mayo analysis rather than relying solely on preemption arguments. See cited case law (e.g., Mayo, Alice, Benson, Flook) for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract Ideas – Enumerated Groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas are grouped to facilitate examination into three enumerated categories: (1) mathematical concepts; (2) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine if a claim limitation recites an abstract idea, (1) identify the specific limitation(s) the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether those limitations fall within at least one of the enumerated groupings. If yes, the claim recites an abstract idea and requires Prong Two analysis. If not, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea. This grouping approach shifts examiners away from a pure case-comparison method and aligns with the body of precedent. See MPEP §2106.04(a)(2) for examples and further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination Must Rely on Full Disclosure and Broadest Reasonable Interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the §101 eligibility analysis examiners must determine what the inventor has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing the claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps 1 and 2A evaluations should be made only after reviewing the application disclosure and applying BRI (see MPEP §2106 subsection II and §2111). This ensures accurate identification of claimed subject matter and whether claim limitations recite or integrate judicial exceptions.
